title: The Spirit made Simeon prophet and temple
english: Do you not know that the Spirit made Simeon a prophet and announced to him as an oracle that he would not see death before seeing the Christ? “Now you are releasing your servant, Master, according to your word, in peace” (Luke 2:29). Was it not by the Spirit’s gift that he blessed Joseph and Mary? Was it not by the Spirit’s command that he spoke to Mary, “Behold, this child is set for the fall and rising of many in Israel” (Luke 2:34)? Was it not through the Spirit that Anna was possessed as a prophetess? Was it not from him that she, filled, proclaimed the redemption that was to come through the infant?

I should have woven the explanation of these things for you point by point, but perhaps the time has been spent, and it is fitting to cut the discourse short out of regard for your obedience. But if this proposal is unbearable to you, since you are fellow guests at the table of the sacred sayings and insatiable, then from the point where the Gospel writer began the story for you, from there it is fitting for us also to cut short the interpretation as far as possible, so that what is offered may suit both the occasion and your longing.

“And behold, there was a man in Jerusalem whose name was Simeon” (Luke 2:25). The Spirit was weaving no small praise for this Simeon in the opening words. “For behold,” it says, “there was a man in Jerusalem” whom the prophets had long sought and the law had desired, and grace found him and, having found him, crowned him with what follows. From where is the crown woven? Pay attention: “And this man was righteous and devout, awaiting the consolation of Israel” (Luke 2:25). It is fitting to envy Simeon and call him blessed, because he was not only righteous but also devout, and he kept away from every evil. And as one “awaiting the consolation of Israel,” he did not grow numb while toiling for the virtues, nor did he grow weary while keeping away from evil.

“And the Holy Spirit was upon him” (Luke 2:25). This too is wonderful and fitting with what has been said before. For he was a temple; he kept the bridal chamber of his flesh clean, and the bridal chamber of his soul was pure of every spiderweb of worldly life. From there he drew to himself the dwelling of the Spirit. “And it had been revealed to him by the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before seeing the Christ of the Lord” (Luke 2:26). Do you see how great a thing it is to be a temple of God? Those who have trained their life in this way pass from life to life. For this reason it had been revealed to Simeon that he would not see death before seeing the Christ of the Lord—that is, before seeing the one who abolishes death, before seeing the one who raises the dead, before seeing the one who turns tombs into bridal chambers, before beholding the one who makes his departure from here fearless.

“And he came in the Spirit into the temple” (Luke 2:27). This too is not worthy to be passed over or run past. For it is proof that he acted according to the command of the indwelling Spirit, and he did not go into marketplaces or any affairs at all without the Spirit. Indeed, he comes into the temple in no other way than with the Spirit leading him by the hand. “And when the parents brought in the child Jesus, to do for him according to the custom of the law, he also received him into his arms” (Luke 2:27–28). Who revealed the infant to him, whom he did not know? It is clear that it was the Spirit dwelling in him and giving him oracles, and surely saying to Simeon: “Run, old man, run; hurry now; quickly seize the blessing, before the star—

The phrase 'οὔτε περὶ τὰς ἀρετὰς κοπιῶν ἐνάρκα, οὐδὲ κακίας ἀπεχόμενος ἔκαμεν' refers to the nuance of his character regarding the striving for virtue and the avoidance of vice.

orientation: Hesychius opens his homily on the Presentation by asking his hearers whether they recognize that the Holy Spirit made Simeon a prophet, blessed through him, and filled Anna to proclaim redemption.
